content: Omeprazole should be stored at room temperature, specifically between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). It can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C), such as during transportation. Always store it in a cool, dry place. Omeprazole is available in various forms, including capsules or tablets that are swallowed, powder that is mixed into liquid and swallowed or administered through a feeding tube, and tablets that dissolve in the mouth. The most common side effects of omeprazole include headache, stomach pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and gas. In children aged 1 to 16 years, it may also cause infections in the nose or throat and fever. If any of these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your healthcare provider if you suspect you are experiencing a side effect. Serious side effects of omeprazole, though less common, include the following: 1. Kidney Problems: Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can occur at any time during treatment. If you notice a decrease in urine output or blood in your urine, contact your doctor immediately. 2. Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea: Overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) in the gut can occur. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, and fever. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if these symptoms arise. 3. Severe Skin Reactions: Omeprazole can cause life-threatening skin conditions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). Symptoms include painful red or purple skin that peels, flat red rashes or blisters on the skin, mouth, nose, or genitals, and red, painful, watery eyes. Stop taking omeprazole and seek emergency medical help if these symptoms occur. 4. Severe Allergic Reaction (DRESS): Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) can affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms include skin rash, hives, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the legs or feet, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Stop using the medication and seek immediate medical attention if these symptoms develop. 5. Lupus: Omeprazole can trigger or worsen lupus, an autoimmune disorder. Symptoms include new or worsening joint pain or a rash on the arms or cheeks. Inform your provider immediately if these occur. 6. Vitamin B-12 Deficiency: Long-term use of omeprazole (3 years or more) can reduce vitamin B-12 absorption, leading to deficiency. Symptoms include a sore tongue, weakness, or tingling/numbness in the hands or feet. Stop using omeprazole and contact your healthcare provider if these symptoms arise. 7. Hypomagnesemia: Omeprazole can cause low magnesium levels, which may lead to seizures or heart rhythm problems. Symptoms include changes in heart rate, dizziness, muscle spasms, or seizures. Stop using the medication and contact your healthcare provider if these occur. 8. Bone Loss and Fractures: Long-term or high-dose use of omeprazole, especially in older adults, may increase the risk of bone loss and fractures. 9. Severe Allergic Reactions: Symptoms include breathing problems, wheezing, a racing heart, fever, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, trouble swallowing, itching, rash, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or joint pain. Stop using omeprazole and seek emergency help if these symptoms occur. Precautions for omeprazole use include the following: Do not use omeprazole if you are allergic to it, any proton pump inhibitors, or any ingredients in the product. Your pharmacist can provide a list of ingredients. Inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are taking, as omeprazole may interact with other drugs. Do not take omeprazole unless prescribed by a healthcare provider. Take it exactly as directed and do not share it with others. Do not chew, cut, or crush omeprazole. Take it before a meal. If you have difficulty swallowing capsules, you may open them and sprinkle the contents on one tablespoon of applesauce, swallowing immediately without mixing with other foods. Omeprazole is not for immediate relief of heartburn and may take 1 to 4 days to work fully. Before using omeprazole, inform your healthcare provider about any health conditions, including low potassium, magnesium, or calcium levels, or liver problems. Also, discuss any medications or supplements you are taking, as omeprazole may interact with them. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, consult your healthcare provider to determine if omeprazole is safe for you. Do not use omeprazole while breastfeeding, as it can pass into breast milk. If you or someone else has taken too much omeprazole, seek medical help immediately, call 911, or contact a Poison Control center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. Omeprazole is used to treat heartburn and conditions caused by excess stomach acid, such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), ulcers, erosive esophagitis, and Helicobacter pylori infections. It works by reducing stomach acid production. Omeprazole is available as Prilosec, Prilosec OTC, and generic forms in various dosage forms, including delayed-release oral suspension powders (5 mg and 10 mg packets).
